scope.current_boundary: Define a couple as a pair of forces that acts to produce rotation only. Identify the four necessary conditions of a couple: equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, parallel lines of action, and separate lines of action. Contrast a couple acting on a single rigid body with a Newton's third law pair acting on two different bodies. Define and calculate the torque of a couple as the product of one of the forces and the perpendicular distance between the lines of action of the forces (torque = F * d). State and use the unit newton metre (N m) and state rotational sense (clockwise or anticlockwise). Identify perpendicular distance across common geometries: diameters for circular discs, perpendicular components for inclined rods, and perpendicular side lengths for right-angled plates. Explain why a couple has zero resultant force (F + (-F) = 0) but non-zero turning effect, proving that zero resultant force does not guarantee equilibrium. Explain that torque is independent of pivot position and invariant when translated across a rigid body. Strict exclusions: do not teach the principle of moments (owned by 9702_t04_cm02_l03); do not teach complete equilibrium conditions combining zero force and zero resultant torque (owned by 9702_t04_cm02_l04); do not construct vector triangles (owned by 9702_t04_cm02_l05).

immediate_next.title: The principle of moments

demands: Formulate an algebraic expression for the torque of a couple acting tangentially at points A and B on a disc of radius r.

misconceptions: Using the radius r instead of the diameter 2r as the distance between the lines of action.
Confusing the torque of a couple with the moment of a single force about the centre O.

demands: Identify the definitive physical characteristics of the two forces forming a couple.

misconceptions: Believing forces in a couple can be perpendicular to each other.

Believing lines of action can pass through the same point.

demands: Determine which force-pair diagram constitutes a genuine couple producing a specific torque of 30 N m.
Apply torque = F * d = 15 N * 2.0 m = 30 N m with equal opposite parallel forces.
misconceptions: Halving the perpendicular separation (e.g. taking 30 N * 1.0 m) or doubling the force.

demands: Calculate the symbolic torque of a couple formed by opposite forces F on a disc of radius r.

misconceptions: Selecting Fr by multiplying one force by the radius rather than the diameter.

demands: Identify which configuration of two parallel forces of magnitude F on a rod yields the maximum torque.
Distinguish couple configurations (opposite directions) from non-couples (same direction) and recognise that torque increases linearly with separation d.
misconceptions: Failing to check force directions and selecting parallel forces pointing in the same direction.

demands: Determine the torque of a couple acting at two vertices of a right-angled triangular plate.
Identify the perpendicular distance between the lines of action as side length y rather than hypotenuse length x, giving torque = Fy.
misconceptions: Using the direct distance between the points of application (hypotenuse x) instead of the perpendicular distance between the lines of action (side y).
Doubling the force to produce 2Fy or 2Fx.

demands: Calculate the torque about pivot P for two opposite forces F at distance d on either side of P.
Evaluate torque = F * (2d) = 2Fd, or sum moments Fd + Fd = 2Fd.
misconceptions: Thinking that equal opposite forces produce zero torque because the forces cancel out.
Considering only one force's moment Fd.
Doubling both force and distance to arrive at 2F * 2d = 4Fd.

demands: Calculate the torque of a couple on a rod where force locations and separation are specified with extra offset dimensions.

misconceptions: Using the total length of the rod (20.0 cm) instead of the separation between the forces.
Doubling the force (using 30 N * 0.050 m = 1.50 N m).
Calculating moments about an unstated end point rather than using couple torque.

demands: State the definition of centre of gravity as the point where all the weight of an object is taken to act.

hook.historical_investigation: Louis Poinsot and the irreducible force pair in statics (1803)
hook.why_this_spine: Prior to Poinsot, 18th-century mechanicians attempted to simplify every system of forces acting on a rigid body down to a single resultant force. When confronted with two equal, opposite, non-collinear forces, the resultant force vector was mathematically zero, yet the object clearly accelerated in rotation. Poinsot solved this apparent paradox in 1803 by introducing the couple as an independent, irreducible mechanical entity with pure turning action, establishing that rotation cannot be reduced to a single linear push.

verified_facts.fact: In 1803, French mathematician Louis Poinsot published 'Éléments de statique' in Paris, formally coining the term 'couple de forces' (couple of forces) for two equal, parallel, opposite forces acting along different lines.
verified_facts.source: Poinsot, L. (1803). Éléments de statique. Paris: Firmin Didot.

verified_facts.fact: Poinsot demonstrated that a couple cannot be replaced by any single equivalent resultant force, because its vector sum is zero while its turning moment is non-zero.
verified_facts.source: Poinsot, L. (1803). Éléments de statique, Section: 'Des couples de forces'.

verified_facts.fact: Poinsot proved that the rotational moment of a couple is identical about every point in space and that a couple can be moved anywhere in its plane on a rigid body without altering its mechanical effect.
verified_facts.source: Poinsot, L. (1803). Éléments de statique, pp. 20-35.

hook.closing_question: Why does shifting the position of a couple anywhere across a rigid body leave its turning effect completely unchanged, while moving a single force completely changes its moment?
